item.title: Ehime Mikan and Citrus: Japan's Orange County — Guide
item.description: Ehime is Japan’s citrus kingdom, a prefecture so associated with the fruit that mikan (mandarin oranges) are practically its emblem. Its warm, sunny climate and steep, sea-facing hillsides — especially around Yawatahama and the Nanyo coast — are covered in terraced orchards producing not just mikan but an astonishing range of citrus: the local iyokan, sweet dekopon, ponkan, kiyomi, blood-red types and many more, ripening in succession through autumn, winter and spring.

item.title: Nagato Citrus: Mikan Picking on the Coast — Guide
item.description: The warm, sunlit coast around Nagato in northern Yamaguchi is ideal citrus country, and the area is known for its mikan — the small, sweet, easy-peel mandarin oranges that are a staple of Japanese autumn and winter. In season, orchards on the hillsides open for fruit picking, letting visitors wander among the trees, pick sun-ripened mikan straight from the branch, and eat their fill of the sweet, juicy fruit. Set against the backdrop of the scenic Nagato coast and the islands offshore, it is a relaxed, family-friendly outing and a refreshing, healthy taste of the region — a gentle counterpoint to Nagato’s dramatic shrine and wilder coastline.

item.title: Wakayama Mikan: Japan's Mandarin Orange Capital — Guide
item.description: Wakayama is Japan’s leading producer of mikan (satsuma mandarin), and the fruit is woven into the prefecture’s identity: the warm, sunny hillsides above the Kii coast are terraced with orange groves that turn the slopes brilliant orange from late autumn, and the region’s Arida district is one of the most famous mikan names in the country. From October through winter, orchards around Arida, Yuasa and the coast open for all-you-can-pick sessions, and roadside stands sell fruit picked that morning — sweeter and juicier than anything found in a supermarket.

item.title: Wakayama Food Guide: Mikan Oranges, Kishu Plums & Kuroshio Seafood
item.description: Wakayama Prefecture’s food identity is inseparable from its geography. The prefecture stretches from the mountains of Koyasan down through deep river valleys to a rugged Pacific coastline swept by the warm Kuroshio Current — one of the ocean’s great fish highways. The warm climate of the Kii Peninsula produces Japan’s finest citrus and most celebrated pickled plums, while the Kuroshio delivers bluefin tuna, spiny lobster, and skipjack caught by fishing fleets that have worked these waters for centuries.

item.title: Ehime Food Guide: Taimeshi, Jakoten, Mikan, and More
item.description: Ehime’s food culture is shaped by two bodies of water: the Seto Inland Sea to the north, which produces superb sea bream and small reef fish, and the warm Pacific-facing coastline to the south, with its aquaculture bays and citrus orchards. The prefecture’s best cooking is honest and ingredient-focused — grilled fish, fried fish paste, rice made extraordinary by what is laid on top of it. This guide covers the dishes you should not leave without eating.

item.title: Ehime Girls Trip: Dogo Onsen Yukata, Mikan Sweets & Matsuyama Trams
item.description: Ehime sits on the northwestern coast of Shikoku, a prefecture whose identity is woven from three distinct threads: Japan’s oldest hot spring, a castle that actually survived intact through the centuries, and enough citrus groves to make mandarin oranges its unofficial symbol. For a group of friends looking to combine genuine cultural texture with indulgence, Matsuyama and its surroundings offer a range of experiences that are hard to find concentrated in one place anywhere else in Japan.
